questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The system prompt says "always verify the customer's identity with get_customer before any refund". Even so, an audit found that about 3% of process_refund calls happened without prior verification. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Reinforce the instruction in the system prompt with capital letters, repeat it at the end of the prompt, and include the compliance rationale, since the model follows rules better when it understands them.
A PreToolUse hook that denies process_refund until the session has a recorded identity verification.
Add three few-shot examples showing the get_customer → process_refund sequence in refund conversations.
Create a second model that reviews each conversation after it closes and flags refunds made without verification.
questoes.explicacao: A critical rule (financial, security, compliance) belongs in code: a PreToolUse hook that denies process_refund until identity is verified. Prompts and few-shot examples are only for what can be best-effort.
feedbacks: Tempting because it usually lowers the error rate, but prompts are probabilistic: the failure still has a non-zero probability. Anti-pattern: a critical business rule enforced by prompt alone.

Correct. A rule with financial consequences requires deterministic enforcement. The hook always blocks, regardless of what the model decides, and the returned reason lets the agent self-correct (verify first, then refund).
Few-shot improves the average pattern, but it is still probabilistic guidance. For a financial and compliance rule, 'almost always' is not enough.
It detects the problem only after the money is gone, and it adds complexity. This is auditing, not prevention. The block has to happen before the tool executes.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

A customer writes in all caps, furious, because he was charged a R$ 8 late fee. Company policy allows late fees of up to R$ 15 to be reversed automatically on the first occurrence, and this is his first time. The customer has not asked to talk to a human. What should the agent do?
opcoes: Escalate immediately with escalate_to_human, since very angry customers tend to be better served by people and the risk of losing the customer is high.
Ask the model to estimate its own confidence from 0 to 1 and escalate if it falls below 0.8.
Offer a discount coupon instead of the reversal, to calm the customer down without touching the charge.
Acknowledge the frustration, apply the reversal provided for in the policy, and confirm the resolution.
questoes.explicacao: Angry customer with a simple issue covered by policy: resolve it. Escalation is based on an explicit request for a human, a policy exception/gap, or lack of progress, not on sentiment.
feedbacks: Tempting because it seems empathetic, but it is the anti-pattern of escalating based on sentiment. The case is simple and resolvable; the escalation trigger is an explicit request, a policy gap, or lack of progress.
Anti-pattern: the model's self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and does not indicate whether the case is covered by policy.
It targets the wrong symptom (the customer's mood) and ignores the policy that actually solves the problem. It also invents an action the policy does not provide for.
Correct. Sentiment is not complexity: the case is fully covered by policy and the agent has the tool to resolve it. Escalating here only hurts the first-contact metric and the experience.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The customer identifies himself as "Carlos Souza", and get_customer returns three records with that name, in different cities. The customer wants to cancel an order. What is the agent's BEST next action?
opcoes: Ask for an additional identifier (email or order number) and repeat the search.
Select the record with the most recent purchase, since it is the most likely to be linked to a cancellation.
Escalate to a human, because identity ambiguity is outside the agent's scope.
List the three records with address and phone number so the customer can choose which one is theirs.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple customers match the search: ask for an identifier to disambiguate. Don't guess, don't expose other customers' data, and don't escalate what can be resolved with one question.
feedbacks: Correct. With multiple results, the agent should disambiguate using a piece of data the customer has, without guessing. It is cheap and avoids acting on the wrong account.
Tempting because of the 'most likely' heuristic, but it is a guess that could cancel someone else's order. Acting on the wrong account is a security and privacy risk.
Unnecessary escalation: the agent can resolve the ambiguity on its own with one question. Escalating here drags down first-contact resolution.
It resolves the ambiguity, but it exposes third parties' personal data. The customer is the one who confirms identity, by providing a piece of data only they have.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

When the order system times out, the lookup_order tool catches the exception and returns {"orders": []}. At those moments, the agent has been telling customers that it "found no orders under your name". Which change fixes the problem at the source?
opcoes: Instruct the agent, in the system prompt, to be suspicious of empty lists and always repeat the query once before answering.
Catch the exception and return the message "Operation failed" with status 500, so the agent at least knows something went wrong and informs the customer.
Return a structured error (isError, errorCategory "transient", isRetryable: true) instead of an empty list.
Increase the timeout of the call to the order system from 5 to 30 seconds.
questoes.explicacao: Anti-pattern: silent suppression (an empty list reported as success when the backend is down). The tool should return a structured error with a category and a retryable indication, separating 'empty' from 'failed'.
feedbacks: It works around the symptom in the wrong place: the model still doesn't know whether the empty list is real or a failure, and repeating legitimate searches that have no results wastes calls.

Better than silencing it, but it is the generic-error anti-pattern: without a category, without knowing whether it is retryable, and without context on what was attempted, the model cannot plan the recovery.
Correct. Empty is information ('nothing found'); a timeout means the search didn't run. The structured error lets the model distinguish the cases, retry, or inform the customer honestly.
It reduces how often the problem happens but doesn't eliminate it: when the timeout does happen, the failure is still disguised as 'no orders'.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

A customer requests a R$ 2,300 refund. process_refund responds with an error saying the amount exceeds the R$ 1,000 limit for automatic refunds, and the agent keeps calling the tool again, sometimes splitting the amount into smaller installments. How should the tool's error response be designed?
opcoes: As a transient error with retry-after, so the agent tries again later.
As a validation error, flagging the amount field as invalid, so the agent corrects the input and resubmits the request with an amount within the allowed limit.
No changes to the tool; just limit the agent to three process_refund calls per conversation.
As a business error: errorCategory "business", isRetryable: false, and the policy rule explained.
questoes.explicacao: Business errors (policy limits) are non-retryable: explain the policy or escalate. The error category guides the agent's recovery strategy.
feedbacks: Wrong category: the limit won't change over time. Misclassifying the error induces exactly the retry loop you want to avoid.
Tempting because the problem 'seems' to be the amount, but it encourages the agent to split the refund to get around the policy, which is precisely the undesired behavior.
An arbitrary limit as the primary mechanism: it cuts the loop, but it doesn't give the model the information to explain the policy or escalate correctly.

Correct. A policy error is not retryable; the category and isRetryable: false tell the model that insisting won't help, and the description lets it explain or escalate (a policy exception is an escalation trigger).

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The agent loop was written like this: if the model's response contains a text block, the conversation ends and the text is sent to the customer. In several cases, the customer receives "I'll check the status of your order" and nothing else. What is the cause, and what is the fix?
opcoes: The response contained text and tool_use; the loop should follow stop_reason, ending only on "end_turn".
The model is ending early; the fix is to instruct it to never write text before calling a tool.
The loop should search the text for closing phrases such as "done" or "resolved" and only end when one of them appears, keeping the rest of the code the same.
max_tokens is too low and cuts off the response; increasing it solves the problem.
questoes.explicacao: Drive the loop by stop_reason: tool_use → execute and return tool_result; end_turn → finish. Text in content does not signal the end.
feedbacks: Correct. content can mix text and tool_use; having text doesn't mean it's finished. stop_reason is the loop's control signal.
It attacks the model's normal behavior instead of the loop bug. Text before tool_use is legitimate; what's wrong is the code that interprets text as the end.
Classic anti-pattern: ending the loop by parsing natural language. It is fragile and still ignores the structured signal that exists for this purpose.
A max_tokens cutoff would show up as stop_reason "max_tokens", not as short text followed by tool_use. Wrong diagnosis.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

In long sessions (40+ turns), the history is summarized automatically to fit in the window. An audit noticed that, after summarization, the agent sometimes cites the wrong order amount (R$ 129 instead of R$ 192) or mixes up the order number. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Switch to a model with a larger context window, eliminating the need to summarize and keeping the entire original conversation history available on every turn.
A persistent block of case facts (IDs, amounts, dates, status) that is never summarized and is re-injected on every turn.
Ask the summarizer to "be more careful with numbers".
Automatically end the conversation after 30 turns and ask the customer to open a new ticket.
questoes.explicacao: Summaries lose exact values, IDs, dates, and percentages. The fix is a persistent CASE FACTS block that is never summarized.
feedbacks: It postpones the problem and increases the cost of every turn; long conversations still degrade (lost in the middle). It doesn't guarantee the accuracy of the numbers.
Correct. Summaries lose precisely the exact values, IDs, and dates. A case facts block that is never summarized preserves what cannot be paraphrased.
A vague, probabilistic criterion. The critical facts still go through paraphrasing, which is the source of the error.
It harms the customer and the first-contact resolution goal, and conversation length is not a valid criterion for closing or escalating.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

Human support agents complain that, when they receive an escalated case, they have to read the entire conversation to understand what happened, and many don't even have access to the full transcript in their tool. What should the agent send along with escalate_to_human?
opcoes: The full conversation transcript, so the human agent has all the context available.
A short sentence with the reason for the escalation, so as not to overload the human agent.
A structured summary: customer, issue, order and amount, root cause, actions taken, and recommended action.
The customer's sentiment score and the model's confidence, so the human agent can prioritize the queue.
questoes.explicacao: A human handoff requires a structured summary: customer, issue, order, root cause, actions taken, reason for the blocker, recommended action, and amount.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is 'complete', but it is exactly what causes rework, and the human agent may not even have a place to read it. It doesn't highlight the cause, the actions taken, or the next action.
Too short: it lacks identity, amounts, actions already taken, and a recommendation; the human agent would have to reconstruct the case.
Correct. The human usually doesn't see the transcript; the handoff needs to be self-contained and structured so they can act without rework.
Metrics of little use for resolving the case (and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated). It doesn't say what happened or what to do.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The MCP server exposes lookup_order ("retrieves order information") and get_shipment ("retrieves order and delivery information"). For tracking questions, the agent picks the wrong tool in about 30% of cases. What is the first fix to try?
opcoes: Rewrite the descriptions to separate their purposes and say when to use each one (or merge the two tools).
Put an intent classifier in front of the agent, trained on labeled conversations, that decides which of the two tools should be used for each question.
Add to the system prompt a list of keywords that point to each tool.
Force tool_choice to get_shipment whenever the customer's message mentions "delivery".
questoes.explicacao: Vague, overlapping descriptions cause wrong selection. The first fix is to improve/differentiate the descriptions (or merge the tools); external classifiers are unnecessary complexity.
feedbacks: Correct. The description is the tool-selection criterion. Overlapping tools with nearly identical descriptions cause misrouting; the simplest fix is to differentiate them (or unify them).
It works, but it is more complex than necessary. The exam's tiebreaker rule: a better description before a routing classifier.
A fragile patch in the wrong place; selection information should be in the tool definition itself, which the model consults at decision time.
It shifts the decision to an external keyword rule (a decision tree outside the model) and fails when 'delivery' appears in another context.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

As the project expanded, the single agent grew to 18 tools (CRM, billing, logistics, knowledge base, coupons, loyalty...). Tool selection got visibly worse, even after the team reviewed all the descriptions. Which architecture solves this best?
opcoes: Sort the tools alphabetically and number them in the system prompt to make selection easier.
Increase max_tokens and enable a higher reasoning effort so the model thinks harder about the selection.
Combine the 18 tools into a single generic execute_action tool with an action parameter, reducing the number of tools the model needs to consider to just one.
Split into specialized subagents with 4–5 tools each, coordinated by an agent that delegates according to the case.
questoes.explicacao: Guideline: 4–5 tools per agent at decision time. With 18 tools, split into specialized subagents; better descriptions alone are not enough.
feedbacks: It doesn't reduce the number of options at decision time; it's cosmetic.
It targets the wrong symptom: the problem is too many overlapping options, not a lack of output space.
It hides the complexity inside a parameter, loses the specific descriptions, and makes input validation worse. Selection is still hard, just less visible now.
Correct. With many visible tools, selection degrades, and improving descriptions alone is not enough. Specialized agents keep few tools at decision time.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The team is listing the agent's rules to decide which ones go in code (hooks) and which can stay in the system prompt. Which TWO rules should be enforced deterministically? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Refunds above R$ 1,000 can only be executed after a supervisor's approval.
The agent should address the customer by first name and keep a friendly tone.
When it makes sense, the agent may suggest products related to the customer's order.
Full card numbers must never reach the model or appear in the history.
The agent should end the conversation by asking whether it can help with anything else.
questoes.explicacao: Rules with financial, security, or compliance consequences go in code (hooks/validation). Style and optional behaviors stay in the prompt.
feedbacks: Correct. Financial consequence: a PreToolUse hook on process_refund denies the call without approval, no matter what the model decides.
A style preference: best-effort, it fits perfectly in the system prompt.
Optional, low-risk behavior; prompt guidance is sufficient.
Correct. A security/compliance requirement: a PostToolUse hook (or the tool itself) masks the data before it enters the context.
An experience rule with no financial or security consequence; it doesn't justify enforcement in code.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The team is defining explicit criteria for the agent to call escalate_to_human immediately. Which TWO signals justify immediate escalation? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Sentiment analysis classifies the customer's message as very negative.
The customer explicitly asks to talk to a person.
The model reports a confidence of 0.4 in its own answer.
The conversation has exceeded 25 messages.
The customer requests a refund past the deadline for a reason the policy does not cover, requiring an exception.
questoes.explicacao: Escalate immediately when the customer asks for a human, when there is a policy gap/exception, or when there is no progress after reasonable attempts. Don't escalate based on sentiment, self-reported confidence, or conversation length.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern: escalating based on sentiment. An irritated customer with a simple case should be handled by the agent.
Correct. An explicit request for a human is an immediate trigger; insisting on resolving it goes against the customer's wishes.
Anti-pattern: self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and is not a reliable trigger.
Conversation length does not by itself indicate complexity or lack of progress; it is not an escalation criterion.
Correct. A policy gap or exception is outside the agent's authority: escalate with a structured handoff.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The model started emitting two lookup_order tool_use blocks in the same response (two of the customer's orders). The loop code sends each tool_result in a separate user message, and the API started rejecting the conversation. How should the loop return the results?
opcoes: In a single user message with just one tool_result that concatenates both responses.
In a single user message with both tool_result blocks, each with the exact tool_use_id of its call.
Turn off parallel use with disable_parallel_tool_use: true, so the model calls one tool per response and the current loop keeps working without changes.
Execute only the first call and ask the model to repeat the second one on the next turn.
questoes.explicacao: Parallel tool use: execute the calls and return all the tool_result blocks in a single user message, each with the exact tool_use_id.
feedbacks: It breaks the one-to-one correspondence with the tool_use_ids; the model doesn't know which result belongs to which call, and the API requires one result per call.
Correct. With parallel calls, all the results go together in a single user message, each referencing its own tool_use_id.
It works around the bug by restricting the model and makes the support session slower; the real defect is the loop's return format.
It leaves a tool_use without a result (the API requires a response for each one) and wastes a turn.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

In one response, the model called get_customer and lookup_order in parallel. get_customer succeeded, but lookup_order threw an exception because the service was unavailable. What should the loop return to the model?
opcoes: Only the get_customer result, omitting lookup_order so as not to confuse the model.
Abort the entire turn and tell the customer that the system is down.
The get_customer result and, for lookup_order, a tool_result with is_error: true and the error description.
Retry lookup_order in code until the service responds and only then return both results together, so the model doesn't have to deal with the failure.
questoes.explicacao: When one parallel call fails, return all the tool_result blocks together, with is_error: true on the one that failed. No omitting results and no aborting everything.
feedbacks: It leaves a tool_use without a response (a protocol error) and hides the failure: silent suppression.
Anti-pattern: aborting the workflow over a partial failure. There is useful data, and the model can retry or proceed with the partial results.
Correct. Every call gets a result; the failed one goes with is_error: true so the model can reason about recovery, making use of the result that succeeded.
Unbounded, invisible retries can stall the support session; bounded backoff is acceptable, but the model needs to know when the failure persists.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

get_customer returns the full customer record: 40 fields, including browsing history and all marketing preferences. In conversations with several lookups, the context bloats and the responses get worse. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Trim the tool's output to the fields relevant to customer support (in the tool or in a PostToolUse hook).
Migrate to a model with a larger context window.
Ask in the system prompt for the model to ignore irrelevant fields.
Summarize the conversation every five turns to free up space.
questoes.explicacao: Trim tool output: return only the relevant fields, not all 40. This preserves context and quality.
feedbacks: Correct. Trim tool output: only the relevant fields enter the context. Less noise, fewer tokens, better attention.
A larger window isn't free (every token is billed on every turn) and doesn't solve the noise that degrades attention.
The tokens remain in the context and still take up attention; the instruction doesn't reduce the volume.
It treats the effect and introduces loss of exact facts in the summary. The cause is the tool's excessive output.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The system prompt says "be flexible with refunds when the case warrants it". Similar cases receive different decisions, and the audit cannot explain the pattern. Which prompt change solves this best?
opcoes: Ask the model to assess the customer's likely satisfaction and grant the refund when it is low.
Lower the temperature to zero, so that similar cases receive exactly the same decision on every run of the agent.
Append "be consistent" to the end of the current instruction.
Replace the instruction with explicit criteria: what is eligible, what is not, and boundary examples.
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria (what counts, what doesn't, boundary examples) beat 'use your good judgment'.
feedbacks: It swaps one vague criterion for another, and one based on sentiment at that. It remains inconsistent.
It targets sampling variation, not the lack of criteria; on recent models, sampling parameters may not even be accepted. The criterion remains undefined.
Yet another vague instruction: it doesn't say what is eligible. The model keeps judging case by case without a yardstick.
Correct. Vague instructions ('be flexible', 'use good judgment') produce inconsistency. Explicit criteria with boundary examples make the decision reproducible and auditable.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

To avoid infinite loops, the agent loop stops after 5 tool calls. Complex cases (a return with an exchange and a partial refund) are being cut off midway, leaving the customer without an answer. Which design is correct?
opcoes: Raise the limit to 15 calls, which covers the complex cases observed.
Ask the model to write "SUPPORT COMPLETED" when it finishes and end the loop when the phrase is detected.
Follow stop_reason (continue on "tool_use", stop on "end_turn"), with a high limit only as a backstop.
Code a decision tree that defines the tool sequence for each type of support case, ensuring every case ends in a predictable number of steps.
questoes.explicacao: stop_reason drives the loop. An iteration limit is acceptable only as a backstop, never as the primary stopping mechanism.
feedbacks: It still uses an arbitrary limit as the primary mechanism; some case will still get cut off, and there is no handling for the cutoff.
Anti-pattern: ending the loop by parsing natural language instead of stop_reason.
Correct. The model decides when to stop, signaling it through stop_reason. An iteration limit is a safety net, not the primary mechanism.
It takes away from the model the decision of which tool to use and when to stop, losing the flexibility for ambiguous cases, which are the agent's strength.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

The team is going to standardize the MCP tools' error responses so that the agent can choose the right recovery on its own. Which TWO fields are most important for this? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The full stack trace of the exception on the server.
Only the numeric HTTP status code returned by the backend.
errorCategory (for example transient, validation, business, permission).
isRetryable, indicating whether trying again might work.
A fixed message "Operation failed, please try again".
questoes.explicacao: A useful structured error carries a category and isRetryable (plus a description, the attempted action, and partial results). A generic error, a raw status code, or a stack trace does not guide recovery.
feedbacks: Costly noise in the context and possible leakage of internal details; it doesn't help the model decide on recovery.
A status code without context on what was attempted: the same 500 can be transient or permanent. Insufficient.
Correct. The category defines the strategy: retry, fix the input, explain the policy, or escalate.
Correct. It prevents pointless retry loops on business/permission errors and authorizes retries on transient ones.
The generic-error anti-pattern, and it also induces retries on errors that are not retryable.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

A customer comes back the next day to continue a support case about an order that, yesterday, was "being picked". Since then, the order has shipped and a partial refund was processed by a human agent. How should the system resume the case?
opcoes: Resume the previous session exactly as it was, since it contains the entire history of the case.
A new session with a structured summary of the case, re-querying the current order status before answering.
Resume the previous session and let the customer say what has changed since yesterday.
Open a new session without any prior context and ask the customer to explain the problem again.
questoes.explicacao: Resuming only makes sense when the tool results are still valid. If the state has changed, start fresh with a structured summary and re-query the data (or, when resuming, explicitly state what changed).
feedbacks: Tempting because of continuity, but the history contains tool results that are no longer valid ('being picked'); resuming without stating what changed leads to wrong answers.
Correct. The tool results from the previous session are stale; starting fresh with a structured summary and fresh data keeps the agent from acting on old state.
It shifts the responsibility for correcting the state onto the customer, who may not even know about the refund made by the human agent.
It avoids stale state, but it loses all the useful context and worsens the experience; the right approach is to carry over a structured summary.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: VarejoMax serves its customers with an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK that uses MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) to resolve returns, billing issues, and account problems. The goal is 80% first-contact resolution, escalating only when necessary.

While monitoring production, the team found support sessions in which the customer received an empty message. In the logs, the API call returned HTTP 200, but the code only read the text from content and sent it. Which check was missing?
opcoes: Check stop_reason before reading content: "refusal" arrives with HTTP 200 and needs its own handling.
Check the response's HTTP status code before reading the content, treating any status other than 200 as a failure, since safety refusals arrive as 4xx errors.
Increase max_tokens, because the response was probably truncated before the text.
Retry automatically whenever content comes back empty, until text is obtained.
questoes.explicacao: A refusal arrives as HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal". Always check stop_reason before consuming content.
feedbacks: Correct. A refusal comes with HTTP 200 and stop_reason "refusal"; code that ignores stop_reason treats it as an empty success.
False premise: the refusal comes with HTTP 200. Checking only the status code lets the problem slip through.
Truncation would show up as stop_reason "max_tokens" with partial text; the diagnosis is only possible by looking at stop_reason, which the code ignores.
It treats the symptom without understanding the cause; with a refusal, repeating the same request tends to repeat the refusal, and it delays the support session.
